name: Trofinetide

lead: Trofinetide is an oral prescription drug for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder. It is a stabilised copy of a small IGF-1 fragment and was approved by the US FDA in March 2023, the first drug approved for the condition.

It shows up in peptide discussions because of its relation to GPE (glypromate). It is thought to dampen neuroinflammation and support neuronal signalling through IGF-1-related pathways. Approval rests on a 12-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in patients aged two and older; no appearance use is documented.

paras: It is given by prescription as an oral treatment for Rett syndrome, under clinician supervision. It is used in that medical setting rather than as a looks product.
Diarrhea and vomiting are the most common adverse effects in trials. It is prescription-only, with limited data in kidney impairment.

angle.text: Trofinetide is an approved prescription drug for Rett syndrome and a GPE analogue, so it comes up in peptide discussions as a relative of glypromate. It is used and studied as a disease treatment, and no appearance use is documented.

lead: Trofinetide (brand names Daybue and Daybue Stix; Daybu in the EU) is an oral prescription medicine for Rett syndrome, a rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder that mainly affects girls and women, in patients aged two years and older. The US FDA approved it in March 2023, making it the first drug approved for the condition.[1][2][3]

It is a synthetic analogue of glycine-proline-glutamate (GPE), the N-terminal tripeptide of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), modified to last longer in the body. It was developed by Neuren Pharmaceuticals and commercialised by Acadia Pharmaceuticals, and was first explored for neuroprotection, for example in stroke and traumatic brain injury.[4][2][2] Its approval rests on a 12-week placebo-controlled phase 3 trial.[4]

Trofinetide is a treatment for a specific disease. It appears among recovery and IGF-1-related compounds because of its derivation from an IGF-1 fragment, but the research concerns communication, behaviour and function in Rett syndrome; no published study examines it for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Oral solution or powder (including via feeding tube)

paras: Trofinetide is indicated for Rett syndrome, caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene and characterised by regression after early development, loss of hand skills and speech, hand stereotypies, impaired walking, seizures, breathing abnormalities and intellectual disability.[5][3] It has orphan drug, fast track and priority review designations in the US and is described as a first-in-class medication.[2]

Before 2023 no therapy directed at core Rett features had been approved, and treatment relied on management of symptoms such as seizures and orthopaedic problems.[6][5] Rett syndrome was first described in 1966, and identification of the MECP2 gene followed in 1999.[6]

In the phase 3 LAVENDER study, 187 females aged 5 to 20 with Rett syndrome received twice-daily oral trofinetide (93) or placebo (94) for 12 weeks. The least squares mean change in the caregiver-rated Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire was -4.9 for trofinetide versus -1.7 for placebo (effect size 0.37), and the clinician-rated Clinical Global Impression-Improvement score was 3.5 versus 3.8 (effect size 0.47). A key secondary measure, the Communication and Symbolic Behavior Scales social composite, changed by -0.1 versus -1.1 (effect size 0.43).[4][7]

A later analysis of the trial reported a benefit over placebo for the ability to communicate.[8] A 40-week open-label extension, LILAC, followed participants aged 5 to 21 and assessed long-term safety.[9]

In LAVENDER, diarrhea occurred in 80.6 percent of trofinetide participants versus 19.1 percent with placebo, mostly mild to moderate; vomiting was the next most common event, and decreased appetite is also reported.[4][2][3] The US label warns of diarrhea, weight loss and vomiting, advises stopping laxatives before starting, and suggests antidiarrheal treatment, fluids and dose interruption or reduction if diarrhea is severe.[10] A caregiver and nurse study examined how gastrointestinal symptoms are managed in practice.[11] Product information is reported not to recommend use in severe renal impairment because of limited data.[3][10]

Trofinetide is a modified form of GPE with a longer half-life. In preclinical models it is reported to engage IGF-1 receptor-associated signalling pathways and to reduce neuroinflammation; it does not correct the underlying MECP2 mutation.[3][12] The US label states that the mechanism by which it exerts therapeutic effects in Rett syndrome is unknown.[10]

According to Wikipedia, it is well absorbed by mouth (bioavailability about 84 percent), is metabolised to an insignificant degree and is excreted in urine, with a short elimination half-life of about 1.5 hours.[2] An exposure-response analysis supported its weight-based dosing.[13]

The compound derives from research on IGF-1 and its cleaved tripeptide GPE for neuroprotection, was first studied for stroke, and then moved to Rett syndrome under Neuren, with Acadia running the pivotal trial.[2][3][2] Phase 2 studies in pediatric (82 participants aged 5 to 15) and adolescent and adult (56 participants) Rett syndrome were published in 2019 and 2017, and Neuren also ran phase 2 studies in Fragile X syndrome and in mild traumatic brain injury.[14][6][15][16][17]

The FDA approved it on 10 March 2023, Health Canada followed in October 2024 per Grokipedia, a powder formulation was approved in late 2025 per Wikipedia, and it is prescription-only in the EU under the name Daybu.[2][3][2]

Its approval was described in the medical literature as the first Rett syndrome therapy, following decades of work on the disorder since its description in 1966.[1][18] Reviews of treatments for autism and other neurodevelopmental conditions place it among emerging targeted therapies.[19] It is sold only under prescription; Wikipedia describes it as prescription-only in the US, Canada and the EU.[2]

Randomized trials include the 2023 phase 3 study in Rett syndrome, phase 2 studies in pediatric and in adolescent/adult Rett syndrome, and a phase 2 placebo-controlled study in Fragile X syndrome.[4][14][6][15] A 40-week open-label extension and a study in younger girls were registered, the latter terminated.[20][21][9] A study of cognitive function during treatment is recruiting.[22] Reviews place it among emerging targeted treatments for neurodevelopmental conditions.[19]

timeline.event: Phase 2 safety study of NNZ-2566 (trofinetide) in Rett syndrome begins.[23]
Phase 2 study in adolescent and adult Rett syndrome published.[6]
Phase 2 pediatric Rett syndrome study published; phase 3 LAVENDER begins in November.[14][24]
